Metabolic investigations conducted under controlled thermal conditions have provided valuable insight into the energetic physiology of Cowan (Microgale cowani). Specifically, respirometry trials performed at 33 °C [T = 33 °C] yielded a maximum basal metabolic rate of 32 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 32 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, which represents the peak resting oxygen consumption recorded for this species, is consistent with the modest energetic demands predicted for a small-bodied tenrecid inhabiting the cool, stable microclimates of the eastern Malagasy highlands. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, resting individuals during their inactive phase, ensuring that the recorded oxygen uptake reflected true basal conditions rather than the elevated metabolic costs associated with digestion or activity. Such a metabolic rate places Microgale cowani among the more energetically conservative members of its genus, an adaptive trait that likely facilitates survival in environments where ambient temperatures can fluctuate substantially on a diel basis despite the overall moderate annual regime of approximately 33 °C.

Reproductive output in Microgale cowani follows a relatively constrained pattern typical of small, seasonal breeders in unpredictable tropical montane habitats. Under laboratory maintenance at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], females produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with litter sizes ranging from 3 to 5 pups [N_R_i = litter sizes ranging from 3 to 5 pups]. This annual reproductive strategy, characterized by a single, moderately sized litter rather than multiple smaller broods, suggests a life history tuned toward high per-offspring investment. The timing of parturition is closely synchronized with the austral summer rains, when invertebrate prey becomes most abundant, thereby maximizing the probability of neonatal survival during the critical early postnatal period. At the moment of parturition, newborn pups are remarkably altricial, weighing approximately 1 gram [Wwb = approximately 1 gram] at birth. This extremely low neonatal mass, about one-tenth of the maternal body weight, is typical of many tenrecid species and imposes a substantial maternal energetic burden during the subsequent lactation phase.

A detailed understanding of the species' physical maturation reveals that females of Microgale cowani ultimately attain an ultimate wet weight of 10.3 grams [Wwi = 10.3 grams] as fully grown adults. This modest body size, among the smallest recorded for any member of the genus Microgale, is accompanied by a suite of physiological and life-history traits that collectively define a slow-paced, energetically conservative lifestyle. The developmental timeline from birth to reproductive competence is surprisingly protracted for an animal of this mass. When reared under stable thermal conditions at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], individuals do not reach puberty until approximately 200 days after birth [tp = approximately 200 days after birth]. This delay in the onset of sexual maturation is considerably longer than that observed in many other small-bodied eutherian mammals of comparable size, suggesting that Microgale cowani invests heavily in somatic growth and structural development before diverting resources toward gametogenesis and reproductive function.

The early developmental milestones that precede reproductive maturity are equally well characterized for this diminutive tenrec. Neonates, which enter the world weighing just 1 gram [Wwb = 1 gram], are entirely dependent on maternal milk for the first several weeks of life. The transition to nutritional independence occurs at weaning, which under controlled conditions at 33 °C [T = 33 °C] takes place at 29 days after birth [tx = 29 days after birth]. At this point, the young animals have grown substantially and begin to consume solid invertebrate prey, although they may continue to associate with the mother for a brief period afterward. Following weaning, the juvenile period extends for several months, during which the young tenrecs refine their foraging skills and accumulate the body reserves necessary to support the eventual transition to adulthood. The relatively late age at weaning, compared to the rapid development seen in some similarly sized insectivores, reflects the slow maturation strategy characteristic of this species.

Longevity data for Microgale cowani remain somewhat provisional due to the difficulty of conducting long-term mark-recapture studies in its rugged high-altitude habitat, but available evidence from captive individuals suggests a maximum lifespan of approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days] and a gestation period that, when measured under the same thermal regime of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], averages 60 days [tg = 60 days] with a range of 58 to 63 days. This estimate of lifespan, equivalent to about six years, is notably extended for a mammal of less than 11 grams adult body mass, situating the species at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum. This relatively prolonged gestation, roughly twice as long as that of a comparably sized murid rodent, indicates a significant intrauterine investment in organogenesis and neonatal development, likely contributing to the advanced state of the pups at parturition despite their remarkably low birth mass.
